prompt: Why must cyclopropane be a rigid, planar molecule?

choices.text: Its three carbon atoms are three points, and three points define a plane
Its carbons are sp2-hybridized, like the carbons of ethylene
choices.why: Cyclopropane is a cycloalkane with only single bonds. Its flatness follows from geometry: three points always lie in one plane.

choices.text: Its C–C bonds are double bonds, which cannot rotate
choices.why: Cyclopropane has only single bonds. They cannot rotate because rotation would break open the ring, not because they are double bonds.

choices.text: Its hydrogens are too crowded to let the ring pucker
choices.why: The section's reason is purely geometric: three carbon atoms define a plane, so there is no other shape the ring could take.

explanation: Cyclopropane must be a rigid, planar molecule because three points (the carbon atoms) define a plane. No bond rotation can take place around a cyclopropane carbon–carbon bond without breaking open the ring (Figure 4.2.1).

prompt: How does rotation around a carbon–carbon bond in cyclopropane compare with rotation in ethane?

choices.text: Ethane's C–C bond rotates, but cyclopropane's cannot rotate without breaking open the ring
Both rotate freely, because both are C–C single bonds
choices.why: A single bond in a ring is tied back on itself through the other ring atoms; turning it would tear the ring apart.

choices.text: Cyclopropane's bonds rotate freely, but ethane's are locked
choices.why: It is the reverse. Open-chain alkanes like ethane have relatively free rotation; cycloalkanes have much less freedom.

choices.text: Neither rotates, because single bonds never rotate
choices.why: Single bonds in open-chain alkanes rotate relatively freely, which is what gives ethane its conformations.

explanation: In contrast with the relatively free rotation around single bonds in open-chain alkanes, rotation occurs around the C–C bond in ethane but is not possible around the C–C bonds in cyclopropane without breaking open the ring (Figure 4.2.1).

prompt: Very large cycloalkane rings are so floppy that they are nearly indistinguishable from open-chain alkanes. From what ring size up (number of carbons) does this apply?
explanation: Larger cycloalkanes have increasing rotational freedom, and very large rings (C25 and up) are so floppy that they are nearly indistinguishable from open-chain alkanes. The common ring sizes, C3–C7, are severely restricted in their motions.

prompt: Which statement about cycloalkane flexibility is correct?

choices.text: The common ring sizes (C3–C7) are severely restricted in their motions, while very large rings are floppy
All cycloalkanes are equally rigid, whatever their size
choices.why: Larger cycloalkanes have increasing rotational freedom; rings of C25 and up are nearly as flexible as open-chain alkanes.

choices.text: Small rings are floppy and large rings are rigid
choices.why: It is the reverse: the smallest rings are the most restricted, and freedom increases with ring size.

choices.text: Cycloalkanes are more flexible than open-chain alkanes
choices.why: One key difference is that cycloalkanes are less flexible than open-chain alkanes, because rotation is limited by the ring.

explanation: Cycloalkanes are less flexible than open-chain alkanes. Larger cycloalkanes have increasing rotational freedom, and very large rings (C25 and up) are nearly indistinguishable from open-chain alkanes, but the common ring sizes (C3–C7) are severely restricted in their molecular motions.

prompt: In which respect is the chemistry of cycloalkanes like that of open-chain alkanes?

choices.text: Both are nonpolar and fairly inert
Both have relatively free rotation around their single bonds
choices.why: This is a key difference, not a similarity: rotation in cycloalkanes is far more restricted than in open-chain alkanes.

choices.text: Both are polar and reactive
choices.why: Alkanes and cycloalkanes contain only C–C and C–H bonds and are nonpolar and fairly inert.

choices.text: Neither can show cis–trans isomerism
choices.why: Substituted cycloalkanes do show cis–trans isomerism, because a ring has a top face and a bottom face.

explanation: In many respects the chemistry of cycloalkanes is like that of open-chain alkanes: both are nonpolar and fairly inert. One important difference is that cycloalkanes are less flexible.

prompt: Why is cis–trans isomerism possible in substituted cycloalkanes?

choices.text: A ring viewed edge-on has a top face and a bottom face, and substituents can sit on the same face or opposite faces
Substituents can be attached to the ring carbons in a different order
choices.why: A different order of connections gives constitutional isomers. Cis and trans isomers have the same connections.

choices.text: The ring rotates quickly between two shapes
choices.why: Cis and trans isomers do not interconvert; the ring cannot rotate its bonds without breaking open.

choices.text: Cycloalkanes contain double bonds
choices.why: Cycloalkanes have only single bonds. The isomerism comes from the ring's two faces.

explanation: Because of their cyclic structures, cycloalkanes have two faces when viewed edge-on, a "top" face and a "bottom" face. As a result, isomerism is possible in substituted cycloalkanes: substituents can be on the same face (cis) or opposite faces (trans).

prompt: How many different 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane isomers are there?
explanation: There are two: one with the two methyl groups on the same face of the ring (cis) and one with them on opposite faces (trans). Both are stable compounds (Figure 4.2.2).

prompt: Can cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane be converted into trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane by bond rotation?

choices.text: No; neither can be converted into the other without breaking and reforming chemical bonds
Yes; they are conformations of one molecule that interconvert rapidly at room temperature
choices.why: That describes the conformations of open-chain alkanes. In the ring, rotation would break it open, so cis and trans are separate, stable compounds.

choices.text: Yes, but only when heated enough to overcome the torsional barrier
choices.why: The obstacle is not a torsional barrier but the ring itself: rotating a ring bond means breaking the ring.

choices.text: Only the cis isomer can be converted, because it is less stable
choices.why: Neither isomer can be converted into the other without breaking and reforming bonds.

explanation: Both 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane isomers are stable compounds, and neither can be converted into the other without breaking and reforming chemical bonds (Figure 4.2.2).

choices.text: Compounds whose atoms are connected in the same order but differ in three-dimensional orientation
Compounds whose atoms are connected in a different order
choices.why: Those are constitutional isomers, such as butane and isobutane.

choices.text: Different conformations of one molecule produced by rotation around single bonds
choices.why: Conformations interconvert by bond rotation; stereoisomers such as the 1,2-dimethylcyclopropanes cannot without breaking bonds.

choices.text: Compounds with the same formula and the same three-dimensional shape
choices.why: Stereoisomers share connectivity but differ in their three-dimensional orientation.

explanation: Compounds with atoms connected in the same order but differing in three-dimensional orientation are called stereochemical isomers, or stereoisomers. The two 1,2-dimethylcyclopropanes are an example.

prompt: What kind of isomers are butane and isobutane, and what kind are cis- and trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane?

choices.text: Butane and isobutane are constitutional isomers; the 1,2-dimethylcyclopropanes are stereoisomers
Both pairs are constitutional isomers
choices.why: The 1,2-dimethylcyclopropanes have the same order of connections; they differ only in spatial orientation.

choices.text: Both pairs are stereoisomers
choices.why: Butane and isobutane have their atoms connected in a different order, which makes them constitutional isomers.

choices.text: Butane and isobutane are stereoisomers; the 1,2-dimethylcyclopropanes are constitutional isomers
choices.why: This swaps the two: different connections means constitutional isomers; same connections, different 3D orientation means stereoisomers.

explanation: Unlike the constitutional isomers butane and isobutane, which have their atoms connected in a different order, the two 1,2-dimethylcyclopropanes have the same order of connections but differ in the spatial orientation of the atoms, so they are stereoisomers.

prompt: What do the prefixes cis- and trans- mean?

choices.text: Cis- means "on the same side"; trans- means "across"
Cis- means "across"; trans- means "on the same side"
choices.why: This swaps them. Cis isomers have both groups on the same face; trans isomers have them on opposite faces.

choices.text: Cis- means "adjacent carbons"; trans- means "non-adjacent carbons"
choices.why: The ring positions are given by the numbers (1,2-, 1,3-); cis and trans describe the faces of the ring, not the positions.

choices.text: Cis- means "more stable"; trans- means "less stable"
choices.why: The prefixes describe geometry, not stability.

explanation: The 1,2-dimethylcyclopropanes are cis–trans isomers, a subclass of stereoisomers. The prefixes cis- (Latin "on the same side") and trans- (Latin "across") distinguish between them.

prompt: A cyclopentane ring is drawn in the plane of the page. C1 carries a bromine on a wedged bond, and C2 carries a methyl group on a wedged bond. What is the compound's name?

choices.text: cis-1-Bromo-2-methylcyclopentane
trans-1-Bromo-2-methylcyclopentane
choices.why: Both wedged bonds point out of the page, so the two groups are on the same face: cis.

choices.text: cis-1-Bromo-3-methylcyclopentane
choices.why: The groups are on neighboring carbons, C1 and C2, so the locants are 1 and 2.

choices.text: 1-Bromo-2-methylcyclopentane, with no prefix needed
choices.why: Groups on two different ring carbons can be on the same or opposite faces, so the cis- or trans- prefix is part of the name.

explanation: A wedged bond protrudes out of the page and a dashed bond recedes into it. Two substituents are cis if both are out of or both into the page, and trans if one is out and one is in. Both groups here are wedged, so the compound is cis-1-bromo-2-methylcyclopentane.

prompt: A cyclohexane ring is drawn in the plane of the page. C1 carries an ethyl group on a wedged bond, and C3 carries a methyl group on a dashed bond. What is the compound's name?

choices.text: trans-1-Ethyl-3-methylcyclohexane
cis-1-Ethyl-3-methylcyclohexane
choices.why: One group is wedged (out of the page) and one is dashed (into the page), so they are on opposite faces: trans.

choices.text: trans-1-Methyl-3-ethylcyclohexane
choices.why: Substituents are cited in alphabetical order, so ethyl comes before methyl and gets locant 1.

choices.text: trans-1-Ethyl-2-methylcyclohexane
choices.why: The methyl is on C3, two carbons from the ethyl, so the locants are 1 and 3.

explanation: In these views a wedged bond protrudes out of the page and a dashed bond recedes into it. One substituent out and one in means trans, so the compound is trans-1-ethyl-3-methylcyclohexane.

prompt: In a ring drawn in the plane of the page, two substituents on different ring carbons are both on dashed bonds. How are they related?

choices.text: Cis, because both recede into the page and so are on the same face
Trans, because dashed bonds point away from the viewer
choices.why: Cis or trans depends on whether the two groups point the same way. Both into the page is the same face, so cis.

choices.text: Neither; cis and trans apply only when one group is wedged
choices.why: The rule is that two substituents are cis if both are out of or both are into the page.

choices.text: It depends on which carbons they are attached to
choices.why: The locants change the numbers in the name, not whether the groups are cis or trans; that is set by the wedges and dashes.

explanation: Two substituents are cis if they are both out of or both into the page, and trans if one is out of and one is into the page. Two dashed bonds both recede into the page, so the groups are cis.
